payload.task_text:
I am writing a comparative analysis of chain-of-thought reasoning methods for my research group. Please look up the chain-of-thought reasoning papers in the arxiv-latex database and help me organize the findings. The database holds several papers, but only five are about chain-of-thought reasoning methods; the others are about word representations and are out of scope. The five reasoning papers, by arXiv ID, are: 2201.11903, 2203.11171, 2205.11916, 2210.03493, and 2305.10601. Use the arxiv-latex tools (get_paper_prompt or get_paper_abstract) with these IDs to retrieve each paper's title and abstract.

Create a Google Sheet called "Reasoning Methods Comparison" with a sheet named "Papers" that lists the reasoning-related papers. The columns should be Title, Year, Method, and Key_Contribution. For the Method column, try to identify the main reasoning approach described in each paper (for example "chain-of-thought prompting", "self-consistency", "zero-shot CoT", "automatic CoT", or "tree of thoughts"). For Key_Contribution, write a brief one-sentence description of the paper's main contribution. Only include papers that are about reasoning methods, not papers about word embeddings or word representations.

Also create a Word document called "Reasoning_Methods_Review.docx" in my workspace. The document should have the title "Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: Methods Comparison" at the top, followed by today's date (2026-03-06). Then include a section for each reasoning paper, mentioning its title and briefly describing its contribution. End with a short conclusion paragraph.

Note: this task has two deliverables — the Google Sheet and the Word document. If you are running as a team of agents, divide the work between agents (for example, assign the spreadsheet to one agent and the Word document to another) or otherwise serialize your writes, so that both deliverables are completed without conflicting writes to the same file.

Task-Solving Rationable with Sub-task Decomposition:
To solve this task efficiently, the main agent itself retrieves the five fixed papers' title and abstract (five light read-only calls, no research wave), freezes one canonical five-row packet, and dispatches exactly one parallel writer wave of two independent deliverable owners.

Before the wave, the main agent resolves the runtime workspace, freezes the five explicit arXiv IDs — 2201.11903, 2203.11171, 2205.11916, 2210.03493, 2305.10601 — and today's required displayed date 2026-03-06. It calls the arxiv-latex abstract/prompt retrieval once per ID, extracts title/year/method label/key contribution from the returned abstracts only, excludes all word-representation material, and freezes five literal rows {arxiv_id, title, year, method, key_contribution} plus per-ID retrieval controls.

Wave 1 — dispatch exactly 2 coder sub-agents in parallel:

1. coder 0 (external-workflow-operator 0): The Google Sheet writer: create a spreadsheet titled exactly "Reasoning Methods Comparison" with exactly one sheet named "Papers" (rename the default sheet or create the named one), write the header row Title, Year, Method, Key_Contribution followed by exactly the five frozen rows, then read the complete range back and return the spreadsheet/sheet IDs, header check and row count. Do not create the Word document.
2. coder 1 (office-report-builder 0): The Word writer: create Reasoning_Methods_Review.docx in the resolved workspace with the title "Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: Methods Comparison", the literal date 2026-03-06, one section per frozen paper mentioning its title and contribution, and a short conclusion paragraph, then read the document outline and text back. Do not create the spreadsheet.

The two writers serialize only through their own distinct files and never touch each other's deliverable. After the wave, the main agent reconciles both read-backs against the frozen packet (five rows/sections each, exact title/date, reasoning-only scope) and calls claim_done. Do not dispatch any further agent and do not add a verification wave.

Task: Create a Google Spreadsheet for a research comparison of chain-of-thought reasoning papers.

Deliverable: A Google Spreadsheet titled exactly "Reasoning Methods Comparison" containing a sheet (tab) named exactly "Papers".

Steps to perform:
1. Create a new spreadsheet with title "Reasoning Methods Comparison" (use create_spreadsheet).
2. Ensure the spreadsheet has exactly one sheet named "Papers". Typical approach: list_sheets on the new spreadsheet, then rename the default "Sheet1" to "Papers" (rename_sheet). Do not leave any extra sheets.
3. Write the table (header row + 5 data rows) into the "Papers" sheet using update_cells or batch_update_cells. Use range A1:D6 with these exact values:

Header row: Title | Year | Method | Key_Contribution

Row 1: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models | 2022 | chain-of-thought prompting | Shows that prompting large language models with exemplars containing chains of intermediate reasoning steps markedly improves performance on complex arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks.

Row 2: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models | 2022 | self-consistency | Proposes self-consistency decoding, which samples a diverse set of reasoning paths and selects the answer that is most consistent across them, replacing naive greedy decoding for chain-of-thought prompting.

Row 3: Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners | 2022 | zero-shot CoT | Demonstrates that simply prepending the prompt "Let's think step by step" enables large language models to perform multi-step reasoning without any few-shot demonstrations.

Row 4: Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models | 2022 | automatic CoT | Proposes Auto-CoT, which automatically constructs few-shot demonstrations with questions and reasoning chains using clustering and zero-shot CoT generation, eliminating manual chain design.

Row 5: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models | 2023 | tree of thoughts | Introduces Tree of Thoughts, a framework that generalizes chain-of-thought prompting into a tree structure, allowing models to explore multiple coherent reasoning paths with search, lookahead, and backtracking.

4. Optionally make the header row bold (formatting is not strictly required; prioritize correct content).

Acceptance criteria: spreadsheet "Reasoning Methods Comparison" exists; it has a sheet named "Papers"; A1:D1 contains the headers Title, Year, Method, Key_Contribution; rows 2–6 contain the five paper rows exactly as specified.

Report back: the spreadsheet ID, the spreadsheet URL (if available), and confirmation that the "Papers" sheet contains the header plus all five rows.
Create reasoning papers Google Sheet

Task: Create a Word document summarizing five chain-of-thought reasoning papers for a research group.

Deliverable: A Word document at absolute path
/workspace/dumps/kimi-code_Qwen3.8-Max/SingleUserTurn-arxiv-latex-reasoning-gsheet/workspace/Reasoning_Methods_Review.docx

Use the word tools (create_document with the absolute path as filename, then add_heading / add_paragraph). You may use filesystem tools to verify the file exists in that workspace directory.

Required content, in this exact order:

1. Document title at the top (heading): "Chain-of-Thought Reasoning: Methods Comparison"
2. A line with today's date: 2026-03-06
3. One section per paper below. For each: a level-2 heading with the paper title, then one short paragraph describing the paper's method and contribution (you may rephrase slightly for flow, but keep the facts as given).

Paper sections (in order):
a) "Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models" (2022, Wei et al.) — Introduces chain-of-thought prompting: providing large language models with few-shot exemplars that include chains of intermediate reasoning steps markedly improves their performance on complex arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks. It established chain-of-thought prompting as a foundational reasoning method for large language models.

b) "Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models" (2022, Wang et al.) — Proposes self-consistency decoding: instead of taking the single greedy reasoning path, the model samples a diverse set of reasoning paths and selects the most consistent answer by marginalizing over them (majority vote), substantially boosting chain-of-thought accuracy.

c) "Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners" (2022, Kojima et al.) — Shows that large language models can perform multi-step reasoning in a zero-shot setting simply by prepending the trigger phrase "Let's think step by step" before each answer, removing the need for hand-crafted few-shot demonstrations.

d) "Automatic Chain of Thought Prompting in Large Language Models" (2022, Zhang et al.) — Proposes Auto-CoT, which automatically constructs few-shot chain-of-thought demonstrations by clustering questions and generating reasoning chains with zero-shot CoT, eliminating the need to manually design reasoning chains.

e) "Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models" (2023, Yao et al.) — Introduces Tree of Thoughts, a framework that generalizes chain-of-thought prompting to a tree structure over coherent units of text ("thoughts"), enabling deliberate exploration with search, lookahead, and backtracking for harder problem-solving tasks.

4. End with a "Conclusion" heading and a short conclusion paragraph (3–5 sentences) tying the five works together: chain-of-thought prompting showed intermediate reasoning steps improve LLM performance; subsequent work removed the need for few-shot exemplars (zero-shot CoT, Auto-CoT), improved decoding robustness (self-consistency), and extended linear chains to structured search (Tree of Thoughts), charting a progression from prompting technique to general deliberative problem-solving framework.

Acceptance criteria: the file Reasoning_Methods_Review.docx exists in the workspace directory; it opens/reads as a valid docx; text extracted from it contains the title, the date "2026-03-06", all five paper titles, and a conclusion paragraph.

Report back: the full file path and a brief confirmation of the verified structure (e.g., outline of headings).
